drivingQuestion: Why is the baraita's 'tent impurity' needed?
outcomeNote: the baraita is needed to exclude the crow reading

segments.he: אִי מִמַּתְנִיתִין, הֲוָה אָמֵינָא: דִּלְמָא מַיְיתֵי עוֹרֵב טוּמְאָה וְשָׁדֵי הָתָם, וְסַגְיָא בְּדַחְלוּלִי בְּעָלְמָא; קָא מַשְׁמַע לַן:
segments.en: The Gemara answers: «If» this is learned «from the mishna» alone, «I would say» that the concern is that «perhaps a crow might bring» a source of «impurity» and perch on the tree’s branches «and throw it there. And» if that were the only concern, «a mere scarecrow [bedaḥlulei] would be sufficient» to frighten the crows away and prevent that type of impurity. Therefore, the tanna of the baraita «teaches us» that the concern is due to impurity imparted in a tent.

moves.summary: from the mishna one might have thought of a crow; the baraita teaches tent impurity
moves.about: from the mishna alone one might think the concern is a crow dropping impurity, solvable by a scarecrow

edges.about: from the mishna alone one might think the concern is a crow dropping impurity, solvable by a scarecrow
edges.proposedPredicate: respond.justifies_necessity_of — «אי ממתניתין הוה אמינא ... קא משמע לן» — answers a redundancy charge by naming the mistaken inference the seemingly superfluous clause forestalls; answers is generic

positions.claim: the baraita excludes the crow reading, for which a scarecrow would suffice
